title: Samsung Q1 2026 - AI through the financial lens
subtitle: HBM, the memory cycle, pricing power and AI capex
openingQuestion: What does AI capex usually affect most strongly at a chip company?
openingOptions: Revenue, margin and the investment cycle
explanation: The wave of investment for artificial intelligence is a familiar cyclical problem in new clothes. Heavy capital spending today reduces free cash flow immediately and only produces revenue several years later, while depreciation starts eating into margins from the moment the plant runs. The risk particular to semiconductors is that every manufacturer reads the same price signal and expands at the same time, so the new capacity tends to hit the market all at once.

realWorldExample.description: A company selling chips and equipment tends to be valued on the memory cycle, its pricing power, and how much capex it is putting in to keep pace with AI.

quiz.question: When is large capex not necessarily a bad thing?
options: When it is lower than depreciation in that period
When it is funded entirely by shareholders' equity
When it creates capacity and future revenue
When it sits below the industry average
quiz.explanation: Whether capex is good or bad depends on the future rate of return it opens up. Spending less than depreciation is a sign of a shrinking asset base rather than of discipline, how it is funded is a separate question from whether it earns its cost, and matching the industry average says nothing about the returns on this particular investment.

quiz.question: A chip company doubles capex to catch the AI wave, but the margin in the latest quarter falls. How should an investor react?
options: Comparing the margin against the prior quarter alone is quite enough
Conclude at once that the business manages costs poorly
Sell the shares because a falling margin is a bad signal
Look at whether this is the investment phase before capacity runs
quiz.explanation: Heavy capex usually puts short-term pressure on margins (depreciation rises at once, while revenue from the new capacity takes time to materialise) - this is the normal lag of an investment cycle, not automatically a bad signal, but you do have to watch whether revenue rises to match in the following quarters.

quiz.question: Why can the margin fall immediately after a semiconductor business raises capex sharply, even though this is not necessarily a bad signal?
options: Because depreciation rises at once while new revenue comes later
Because selling prices are cut as soon as the new investment starts
Because interest cost on the investment is booked into cost of sales
Because the tax rate applied rises when fixed assets increase
quiz.explanation: This is the natural lag between investment and revenue. You need to follow the next few quarters to see whether revenue rises to match, before concluding whether the investment was good or bad. Prices are set by supply and demand rather than by one company's spending, and neither interest nor tax works the way the other options suggest.

quiz.question: Which particular risk makes the AI investment wave in semiconductors and memory even harder to predict?
options: Semiconductor technology changes so machines become obsolete very fast
Many players invest ahead at once, so oversupply follows
AI demand is only seasonal, quarter by quarter through the year
Governments may withdraw their support packages for the sector
quiz.explanation: Semiconductors and memory are already strongly cyclical; everyone investing ahead of the same trend at once adds the risk of oversupply if real demand arrives later or smaller than the whole industry expected. Obsolescence is a real cost but a predictable one, planned into the depreciation schedule.

quiz.question: Why does the memory semiconductor industry usually fall into an oversupply cycle after each demand boom?
options: Because the cost per chip rises as total industry output rises
Because memory demand falls right as the new plants come online
Because all makers expand capacity and all ship at the same time
Because makers must sell below cost under anti-dumping rules
quiz.explanation: A high price sends the same signal to every manufacturer, and they all react the same way. A plant takes two to three years to build, so the new capacity arrives together - usually just after the demand wave has passed its peak, and the price falls very fast because variable costs are low. Cost per chip in fact falls with scale, which makes the incentive to build stronger, not weaker.

keyTakeaways: AI changes the capex cycle and pricing power
Reading a chip company means reading both the cycle and demand
Capex is only worth it if it generates good enough future cash

practicePrompt.question: Samsung's Q1 2026 financial analysis shows tens of billions of dollars of capital spending on HBM (High Bandwidth Memory) chips. What strategy does that reflect?
options: Getting ahead of the AI memory chip cycle
Scaling down semiconductor production
Switching into the property business
Withdrawing from the smartphone business
practicePrompt.explanation: Heavy capex on HBM shows Samsung's strategic investment direction in taking the AI memory chip supply chain for the big technology names such as NVIDIA and AMD.

sections.text: The AI investment wave is changing how semiconductor and memory companies spend capital - and its effect on corporate finances is far more complex than 'more capex is good'.
AI capex and the lag between investment and revenue

Heavy capex to catch the AI wave can create short-term pressure on margins, because depreciation rises immediately while revenue from the new production capacity takes time to materialise fully. This is the normal lag of an investment cycle and not automatically a bad signal - but you do need to watch whether revenue rises to match in the following quarters.

items: AI capex affects a chip company's revenue, margin and investment cycle all at once
Large capex is not automatically bad if it genuinely creates production capacity and future revenue
A margin falling right after a sharp rise in capex needs following, not a hasty conclusion

sections.text: Why rising capex is not automatically a good or a bad signal

Depreciation on the new investment starts eating into the margin as soon as the asset comes into operation, while revenue from the new capacity takes time to fill - anything from a few quarters to a few years depending on the customers' ordering cycle. This is the natural lag of a heavy-industry investment cycle, not immediate evidence of whether that investment was good or bad.

left.label: Capex that creates value
left.text: The new capacity fills as planned, revenue in the following quarters rises in step with the rise in depreciation, and the ROIC on the new investment beats the cost of capital once it has settled.

right.label: Capex that destroys value
right.text: The investment gets ahead of the cycle but the demand does not arrive as expected - or arrives far later than the depreciation schedule - so the margin is eroded for a long stretch with no revenue to offset it.

sections.label: What makes it worse in semiconductors and memory
sections.text: This is already an industry with a strong cycle in supply, demand and selling price, even without a new investment wave. When many businesses pour capital in ahead of the same trend such as AI, the risk of future oversupply rises considerably if real demand turns out smaller than forecast - the history of this industry has plenty of cycles of overinvestment followed by collapsing prices.

lines: A sharp rise in capex is not always an immediately good or bad signal.
It takes time to know whether that investment really produces matching revenue.
